subject: Degrees of freedom from chi-square GOF

messages.author: 43355b2b15952866
messages.subject: Degrees of freedom from chi-square GOF
parts:
My main question is about how Distance generates the degrees of freedom for a chi-square GOF test, and if I should be concerned by " No Degrees of Freedom for the test. No test possible." appearing under my table in my Chi-sq GOF Test page of my output. The question might be as simple as that, but I'm going to include some details on my data below in case it's relevant.

Some details on the data I'm working with: I have avian point count data for a number of geographical locations (sites) from two years. I imported everything in one sheet from Excel. There are over a thousand lines of data, that is, individual clusters (or individuals) of birds. I've run analyses on pooled data and also data by year using filters.

For every model set, I run CDS, post-stratified by Site ID (there are about 12 sites for each year, some of them appearing in both years). Density is estimated at the global and stratum levels, encounter rate stratum only, detection function global only, and cluster size stratum only. I run five detection function models selected using AICc: Uniform Cosine, Uniform Simple Polynomial, Half-normal Cosine, Half-normal Hermite Polynomial, and Hazard-rate Cosine. I believe everything else in the model definition is set at default. For my data filters, I apply appropriate filters if I'm only looking at one year at a time, I truncate and discard observations beyond 100 m, and then I set my number of intervals. The intervals are the only thing I change between models. I generally run 3-8 intervals and let Distance generate exact bin sizes within 100 m, then choose the best results based on the GOF figures as long as the density/abundance estimates are reasonable (i.e. not 60,000 birds per ha).

In my chi-sq GOF Test page, I get the same message below my table for all models using 6 bins or fewer: No Degrees of Freedom for the test. No test possible. At 7 bins, my df = 4. At 8 bins, my df = 2. 9 bins, df = 3. 10 bins, df = 4 again. I just can't find a pattern. I'd really appreciate any insight. Thanks in advance!

Kristen

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Degrees of freedom from chi-square GOF
parts:
Kristen

Thanks for your thorough description of your analysis.  As is often the case, I'll suggest a different approach to your analysis that circumvents your specific degrees of freedom question, but I'll return to the degrees of freedom question at the end of this message.

The detections in the field, I presume were measured exactly (otherwise you would be unlikely to re-adjust your bin widths between 3 and 8).  If the distance measures are exact, then I suggest you use the goodness of fit measures derived from the QQ plots produced by Distance, namely the Kolomogorov-Smirnov or Cramer von Mises tests.  Using exact distances to assess fit avoids the subjective aspect of selecting the 'proper' number of bins and locations of cutpoints.  The only reason to convert exact distances to grouped distances is if there is a problem in the data collection/recording caused by rounding.

Back to your challenge with deducing degrees of freedom for repeated analyses with varying numbers of bins.  For binned (or grouped) data, the degrees of freedom of the chi-square test is defined as u-q-1, where u is the number of bins and q is the number of parameters in the detection function.  The tricky part is the number of parameters in the detection function when using adjustment terms.  You noted the use of cosine, simple and Hermite polynomial adjustments in your fitting.  The number of parameters in the detection function will depend not only upon the number of parameters in the key function (0 for uniform, 1 for half normal and 2 for hazard rate) but also upon the number of adjustment terms used.  The number of adjustment terms is chosen by the Distance software so you will need to read the model output closely to determine the number of adjustment terms associated with the chosen model.  Moving the cutpoints will change the shape of the histogram of detections, resulting in differing numbers of adjustment terms being selected.

Section 5.1.4 of Buckland et al. (2015) discusses the topic of goodness of fit in more detail.

Buckland, S., E. Rexstad, T. Marques and C. Oedekoven. 2015. Distance Sampling: Methods and Applications. Springer.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Degrees of freedom from chi-square GOF
parts:
Eric,

Thanks for the reply. You're right that I used exact distances when collecting my data in the field, so I will focus on other measures of GOF to choose a model and not worry if there are too few df for the chi-square test.

Thanks again!
Kristen
